summary: Specifies several basic forward error correction schemes for the Reliable Multicast Transport building block, including the compact no-code, small block, large block, expandable, and small block systematic schemes. This is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3452 and RFC 3695.

plainLanguage.summary: Forward error correction means sending extra pieces of data that the receiver can use to rebuild what was lost. This document defines how to label those pieces and how to describe the file they belong to, in four different schemes that other protocols can build on.

subtitle: Four ways to label and describe repair data so a receiver can rebuild a lost file without asking for it again.

tldr.problem: A multicast sender that loses packets normally has to wait for retransmissions, which is slow for a one-to-many transfer. Forward error correction avoids that by sending repair data along with the file, but every content delivery protocol needs a precise way to label that data.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four FEC schemes, each with a fixed FEC Payload ID layout, an FEC Object Transmission Information structure and an FEC Encoding ID: 0 for Compact No-Code, 128 for Small Block, Large Block and Expandable, 129 for Small Block Systematic and 130 for Compact FEC.
tldr.outcome: Only the Compact No-Code scheme is fully specified; the other three leave the actual repair algorithm to the instance that uses them. The document obsoletes RFC 3695, takes over the schemes of RFC 3452, and adds one new rule: all encoding symbols of an object have the same length.

today: RFC 5445 is a Proposed Standard from March 2009. It obsoletes RFC 3695 and takes over the FEC schemes of RFC 3452, which had already been obsoleted by RFC 5052. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Four Schemes and Where They Come From
sections.content:
The document specifies four FEC Schemes according to the specification requirements of the FEC building block of RFC 5052: the Compact No-Code FEC Scheme, the Small Block, Large Block, and Expandable FEC Scheme, the Small Block Systematic FEC Scheme, and the Compact FEC Scheme. It inherits the context, language, declarations and restrictions of the FEC building block, and uses the terminology of RFC 3453, which describes the use of FEC codes within reliable IP multicast transport and introduces some commonly used FEC codes. Building blocks are defined in RFC 3048.

The same schemes first appeared in RFC 3452 and RFC 3695, both published in the Experimental category. This document obsoletes RFC 3695. RFC 3452 had already been obsoleted by RFC 5052, so this document assumes responsibility for aspects of RFC 3452 that RFC 5052 did not include. It is based on, and backwards compatible with, the FEC Schemes defined in RFC 3452 and RFC 3695, updated according to accumulated experience and growing protocol maturity since their original publication.

One scheme is Fully-Specified: everything needed to interoperate is written down. The other three are Under-Specified: this document defines the packet and object formats, but the actual FEC code and the mapping of Encoding Symbol IDs to encoding symbols belong to specific instances, identified by an FEC Instance ID, and their details may even be proprietary. Integer fields in all the schemes are encoded in network byte order.
sections.plainLanguage: Three of the four schemes only describe the envelope around the repair data; the repair method itself belongs to whoever uses the scheme. Only the simplest scheme is written out in full.

sections.title: The Compact No-Code Scheme
sections.content:
The Compact No-Code FEC Scheme is Fully-Specified and requires no FEC coding. It is specified primarily to allow simple interoperability testing between different implementations of protocol instantiations that use the FEC building block.

Its FEC Payload ID is a 16-bit Source Block Number followed by a 16-bit Encoding Symbol ID. The Source Block Number identifies which source block of the object the encoding symbol was generated from. There are two modes: in the unique Source Block Number mode each source block has its own number, starting at 0 for the first source block, so there are at most 2^16 source blocks in the object; in the non-unique mode the same number may be used for more than one source block, and the mapping must be communicated out of band. In that mode, packets for two different source blocks mapped to the same number SHOULD NOT be sent within an interval shorter than the transport time of a source block, so the receiver can tell which packets belong together. Which mode is in use is outside the scope of the document and must be communicated out of band.

The mandatory FEC Object Transmission Information element is the FEC Encoding ID, which is zero for this scheme. The common elements are the Transfer Length, a non-negative integer less than 2^48 giving the length of the object in octets, the Encoding Symbol Length, less than 2^16 octets, and the Maximum Source Block Length, less than 2^32 source symbols. All Encoding Symbols of a transport object MUST have the length given by the Encoding Symbol Length, with the optional exception of the last source symbol of the last source block. That last symbol must be logically padded with zeroes when another Encoding Symbol is computed from it, so the sender and the receiver interpret it the same way, though the padding need not be sent. The Reserved field must be set to zero by senders and ignored by receivers.
sections.plainLanguage: The simplest scheme does no repair maths at all: it just cuts the file into equal pieces and numbers them. Each packet says which block it belongs to and which piece it carries.

sections.title: Source Blocks and the Carousel Procedure
sections.content:
The Compact No-Code scheme requires no FEC encoding or decoding. Each encoding symbol is a run of consecutive bytes of a source block. Let X be the length of a source block in bytes and L the length of the encoding symbol carried in each packet; both are part of the FEC Object Transmission Information. For a source block of X bytes with Source Block Number I, N is X divided by L, rounded up. The source block is logically partitioned into N encoding symbols of L bytes each, with Encoding Symbol IDs from 0 through N-1, and the symbol with ID Y holds bytes L*Y through L*(Y+1)-1 of the source block. If X divided by L is not integral, the last symbol, with ID N-1, holds bytes L*(N-1) through the last byte X-1, and the remaining L*N - X bytes can be padded out with zeroes.

The RFC's example: with a source block length X = 20,400 and an encoding symbol length L = 1,000, the encoding symbol with ID 10 contains bytes 10,000 through 10,999, and the encoding symbol with ID 20 contains bytes 20,000 through the last byte 20,399, with the remaining 600 bytes padded with zeroes.

A carousel procedure is RECOMMENDED for the sender. It sets L to a fixed value that is reasonable for a packet payload, for example one that keeps the total packet size within the MTU, and smaller than the source block length. It initializes Y to a value randomly chosen in the interval [0..N-1], then for each packet generates encoding symbol Y, sets the Source Block Number to I and the Encoding Symbol ID to Y in the FEC Payload ID, and increments Y, wrapping from N-1 back to zero.

The matching receiver procedure is also RECOMMENDED. On the first FEC Payload ID for a source block, the receiver uses the Source Block Length and Encoding Symbol Length received out of band to determine X and L, allocates space for the X bytes, and computes the symbol length by subtracting the packet header length from the total packet length, checking that it equals L, except for the last symbol of the block, which may be shorter. It computes N the same way and allocates a boolean array RECEIVED[0..N-1] with all entries false. For each packet it copies the symbol into the right place and sets RECEIVED[Y] to true; when all N entries are true the whole source block has been recovered.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender walks around the list of pieces of a block, starting at a random point, and keeps going round. The receiver ticks off each piece it gets. When every tick is set, the block is complete.

sections.title: Small Block, Large Block and Expandable
sections.content:
This section defines an Under-Specified FEC Scheme for Small Block FEC codes, Large Block FEC codes and Expandable FEC codes. Its FEC Payload ID is a 32-bit Source Block Number followed by a 32-bit Encoding Symbol ID. The blocks are numbered consecutively from 0 to N-1, where N is the number of source blocks in the object. The details of the correspondence between Encoding Symbol IDs and the encoding symbols in the payload depend on the particular scheme instance, identified by the FEC Encoding ID and the FEC Instance ID, and may be proprietary.

The mandatory FEC Object Transmission Information element is the FEC Encoding ID, which is 128. The common elements are the FEC Instance ID, a non-negative integer less than 2^16, the Transfer Length less than 2^48, the Encoding Symbol Length less than 2^16, and the Maximum Source Block Length less than 2^32. They are encoded as unsigned integers of 48, 16, 16 and 32 bits.

The Scheme-Specific FEC Object Transmission Information allows for instance-specific information. Its first sub-field is a Length of one octet, giving the length of the Scheme-Specific FEC OTI in four-octet words including the length field itself, except that a value of zero indicates that no instance-specific information is provided, in which case three padding bytes containing zero must follow to maintain 4-octet alignment. The rest of the field holds instance-specific information. In the case of a content delivery protocol that supports external signalling of the total FEC OTI length, this field is optional; otherwise it must be included. The algorithm of Section 9.1 of RFC 5052 must be used to partition the file into source blocks.
sections.plainLanguage: This scheme uses bigger numbers, because a file can have many more blocks. It also leaves a fixed-length slot for the user of the scheme to put extra information in.

sections.title: Small Block Systematic and Compact Schemes
sections.content:
The Small Block Systematic FEC Scheme is Under-Specified and covers Small Block Systematic FEC codes, for which each source block is at most 65535 source symbols long. A separate FEC Encoding ID is defined for these codes, 129, to allow more flexibility and retain header compactness: the small source block length and small expansion factor that often characterize systematic codes may require the data source to change the source block length frequently, so the block length is included in the FEC Payload ID.

Its FEC Payload ID is a 32-bit Source Block Number, a 16-bit Source Block Length giving the length in source symbols of that block, and a 16-bit Encoding Symbol ID. Each encoding symbol is either an original source symbol or a redundant symbol generated by the encoder. The common FEC OTI elements are the FEC Instance ID less than 2^16, the Transfer Length less than 2^48, the Encoding Symbol Length less than 2^16, the Maximum Source Block Length less than 2^16, and the Max-Number-of-Encoding-Symbols, less than 2^16, giving the maximum number of encoding symbols per block, that is source plus repair symbols in the case of a systematic code. All Encoding Symbols of a transport object must have the length given by the Encoding Symbol Length, with the same exception for the last source symbol of the last source block. The Scheme-Specific FEC OTI format of Section 4.2.2.3 must be used. The RFC 5052 partitioning algorithm may be used; otherwise the scheme instance must specify the algorithm it uses.

The Compact FEC Scheme is also Under-Specified. It is similar in spirit to the Compact No-Code scheme, except that a non-trivial FEC encoding may be used to generate the encoding symbols placed in the payload of each packet, and a corresponding FEC decoder may be used to produce the source block from the received packets. Its FEC Payload ID format is the one defined for the Compact No-Code scheme, its mandatory FEC Encoding ID is 130, its common FEC OTI elements are the same as for the Small Block, Large Block and Expandable scheme, and it uses the same Scheme-Specific FEC OTI format. The RFC 5052 partitioning algorithm must be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The systematic scheme writes the size of the block on every packet, because the block size changes from one to the next. The compact scheme keeps the small layout but lets the repair data be computed by a real algorithm.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The specification does not introduce any further security considerations beyond those described in the FEC building block of RFC 5052.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is added here. The security questions for repair data are the ones already answered by the building block document.

sections.title: The Registered Encoding IDs
sections.content:
FEC Encoding IDs 0 and 130 were first defined and registered in the ietf:rmt:fec:encoding namespace by RFC 3695, and IDs 128 and 129 by RFC 3452. This document updates and obsoletes those definitions, and references to the old specifications should be replaced with references to this document.

ID 0 is assigned to Compact No-Code, which is Fully-Specified. IDs 128, 129 and 130 are Under-Specified, so FEC Instance ID sub-namespaces must be established for them, in accordance with RFC 5052, and this document assumes responsibility for the ietf:rmt:fec:encoding:instance:128, :129 and :130 registries. The values assigned within these namespaces are non-negative numeric indices, and assignment requests are granted on a First Come First Served basis, subject to the additional criteria of RFC 5052.
sections.plainLanguage: Each scheme gets a number in an official list. The three flexible schemes also get their own sub-lists, so that two users of the same scheme cannot pick the same name for different repair methods.

sections.title: What Changed From RFC 3452 and RFC 3695
sections.content:
The document lists three changes against the Experimental versions. Scheme definitions have been updated to meet the requirements of RFC 5052. Complete encoding formats for the FEC Object Transmission Information for each scheme are now defined here instead of within content delivery protocol specifications, since the exact format depends on the FEC Scheme.

The third change is a new requirement that all encoding symbols of the object have the same length, which the previous specifications for the Compact No-Code and Small Block Systematic schemes did not require. Since no protocols have been defined that support variation of the encoding symbol length within an object, the document argues this should not cause backwards compatibility issues.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules were tidied up to match the newer building block, the formats were pulled into this one document, and one new rule was added: every piece of an object has the same size.
